name: Globe and Mail cryptic crossword No 3,218

clue.text: Sport that Lion developed involving resistance

indicators.note: something developed has grown into a new form, so the letters take a new arrangement
to involve is to take in, so one piece is drawn inside the others

blocks.note: taken as written
R is the physics symbol for electrical resistance

explanation.surface: A lion at the zoo has somehow developed a sport that involves pushing against resistance.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Lion' looks like an animal but is just letters; with R added, THAT LION rearranges to TRIATHLON.
explanation.definitionFit: A triathlon is an endurance sporting event combining swimming, cycling and running in sequence.

clue.text: Samples tagliatelle on vacation somewhere in Italy

indicators.note: a place on vacation is emptied of its occupants, so the word keeps only its shell

blocks.note: to sample food is to try it
the pasta's first and last letters

explanation.surface: A tourist tastes the pasta while holidaying somewhere in Italy.
explanation.walkthrough: 'On vacation' sounds like the tourist's holiday, but it means emptying the word: tagliatelle with its middle gone leaves TE.
explanation.definitionFit: Trieste is a port city in north-eastern Italy, on the Adriatic near the Slovenian border.

clue.text: Quite afflicted state

blocks.note: afflicted with a disease means sick
to state something is to say it

explanation.walkthrough: 'Quite' here is the emphatic exclamation of agreement ('Quite!'), not the adverb meaning fairly; 'state' is a verb, not a nation.
explanation.definitionFit: Both are spoken interjections expressing hearty agreement with what someone has just remarked.

clue.text: Ancient character’s a spiky thing

blocks.note: first meaning: an Old English runic letter, written þ, for the 'th' sound
second meaning: a sharp point on the stem of a rose or bramble

explanation.surface: Some old figure from history turns out to be prickly.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Ancient character' suggests an old person, but character here means a written letter, one used in Old English and Icelandic.
explanation.definitionFit: The same word names an obsolete alphabet letter and a sharp woody spine growing on plant stems.

clue.text: Meat reduced to pound

indicators.note: a reduced thing has been cut short, so the word loses its final letter

blocks.note: lamb is the meat of a young sheep

explanation.surface: Meat is tenderised by being beaten down to a pulp.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Reduced' sounds like cooking a sauce down, but it trims the last letter. 'Pound' is the verb to beat, not money or weight.
explanation.definitionFit: To lam someone is an informal verb meaning to beat or thrash them hard.

clue.text: No news there, I broadcast, still in ignorance

indicators.note: broadcast seed is scattered widely, so the letters are thrown into a new order

blocks.note: taken as written

explanation.surface: A newsreader admits there's nothing to report, so the audience learns nothing.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Broadcast' fits the news surface so well it looks like a verb about radio; it is the anagram signal.
explanation.definitionFit: Being none the wiser is an idiom for having gained no understanding after some explanation.

clue.text: Doorkeeper and drug dealer leaving quietly

indicators.note: what leaves is no longer present, so that letter is dropped

blocks.note: a pusher sells illegal drugs
p (piano) is the musical marking for quiet

explanation.surface: A bouncer and a dealer slip out of a club without a fuss.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Quietly' reads as how the dealer leaves, but it is the letter P that leaves the word.
explanation.definitionFit: An usher guards a door in a court or shows people to their seats, a traditional doorkeeping role.

clue.text: Writer in university’s meeting editor without permission

indicators.note: one thing in another sits inside it, so a piece goes into the middle of another
things meeting come together end to end, so pieces join side by side

blocks.note: UNI is short for university, plus the 's as IS
an author is a writer
ED is the standard abbreviation for editor

explanation.surface: A campus writer gets into a meeting with an editor without being authorised to attend.
explanation.walkthrough: The 's of university's is read as 'is', supplying letters rather than showing possession; 'meeting' only sets the editor alongside.
explanation.definitionFit: Something unauthorised has not been officially sanctioned, so it is done lacking any approval.

clue.text: Violent, aggressive person owned box containing ecstasy

indicators.note: to contain is to hold inside, so one piece goes within another

blocks.note: had is the past tense of have, to own
E is slang for the drug ecstasy
a case is a box

explanation.surface: A thug was found with a box of ecstasy pills.
explanation.walkthrough: The surface suggests the box holds the drug, but the ecstasy goes inside the word for owned. 'Box' also tempts as a verb (to fight) given the violent picture.
explanation.definitionFit: Headcase is British slang for someone unstable and dangerously unpredictable, liable to lash out.

clue.text: Unusual flies circling old chap’s insular location

indicators.note: something unusual is out of the ordinary, so these letters leave their usual order
to circle something is to go round it, so one piece is surrounded

blocks.note: taken as written
O is the standard abbreviation for old
a chap is a man; the 's is 'has', joining

explanation.surface: Strange insects buzz around an old fellow's island home.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Flies' looks like insects but is anagram fodder. The Isle of Man is a self-governing island in the Irish Sea between Britain and Ireland.
explanation.definitionFit: Insular means relating to an island, so an insular location is an island place.

clue.text: Saying taken from go-ahead agency

indicators.note: what is taken from something is lifted out of it, so the letters come straight out of the text

blocks.note: the letters run across the join of the two words

explanation.surface: A dynamic firm's slogan is borrowed for a quote.
explanation.walkthrough: The answer straddles the end of 'go-ahead' and the start of 'agency'.
explanation.definitionFit: An adage is a proverb or traditional maxim, a short memorable statement of common wisdom.

clue.text: Party platform ignoring last thing affected by Reform

indicators.note: ignoring the last letter means leaving off the end of the word
reform means to form anew, so being changed by it puts letters in a new order

blocks.note: a stage is a raised platform
taken as written

explanation.surface: A political party's manifesto is overhauled under Reform, the last item dropped.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Party' and 'Reform' suggest politics (Reform UK is a British party), but Party is the definition and Reform an anagram signal.
explanation.definitionFit: A stag night is a celebration held for a man shortly before his wedding, the British bachelor party.

clue.text: Cheerful Simon regularly observed 51 plants

indicators.note: observing regularly means looking at fixed intervals, so only every other letter is kept

blocks.note: glad means happy
second and fourth letters of the name
LI is 51 in Roman numerals

explanation.surface: A happy gardener named Simon kept watch over 51 of his plants.
explanation.walkthrough: The number is Roman numerals, a common crossword device.
explanation.definitionFit: Gladioli are tall flowering garden bulbs with sword-shaped leaves, so they are plants.

clue.text: Woman’s concealing corroded radiator?

indicators.note: to conceal is to hide inside, so one piece sits within another

blocks.note: her is a pronoun for a woman
rust ate the metal, i.e. corroded it

explanation.surface: A woman hides a rusted radiator from view.
explanation.walkthrough: Corroded means 'ate away at', giving the past tense of eat. The question mark flags that a radiator is just one example of the answer.
explanation.definitionFit: A radiator warms a room, making it one kind of heating appliance, hence the question mark.

clue.text: Fix fight against European

blocks.note: a scrap is a fight
E is the abbreviation for European

explanation.surface: A match against a European side is rigged.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Fix' looks like a verb (to rig a fight) but is a noun: a tight spot.
explanation.definitionFit: Being in a fix or a scrape both mean being in an awkward predicament or trouble.

clue.text: Tory visitor avoiding United crowd

indicators.note: to avoid something is to stay clear of it, so that letter is left out

blocks.note: CON is short for Conservative, the British Tory party
a guest is a visitor
U is the abbreviation for United, as in team names

explanation.surface: A Conservative visitor steers clear of the Manchester United crowd.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Crowd' looks like a noun (football fans) but is a verb.
explanation.definitionFit: To congest a space is to overfill or clog it, much as people crowd a street.

clue.text: Travel up with Heather casting amorous glances

indicators.note: in a down clue, going up means reading from bottom to top

blocks.note: to travel is to go
ling is another name for common heather

explanation.surface: Someone drives up with a woman named Heather, making eyes at her.
explanation.walkthrough: Heather is capitalised to look like a name, but it is the plant, also called ling.
explanation.definitionFit: Ogling means staring at someone with obvious lustful interest, the same as making eyes at them.

clue.text: Reportedly study good article on gold musical instrument

indicators.note: what is reported is passed on by word of mouth, so the sound counts, not the spelling
in an across clue, one thing on another is placed after it, so the earlier-named pieces go second

blocks.note: to read is to study
or is the heraldic term for gold
G is the abbreviation for good
an is the indefinite article

explanation.surface: Someone reportedly studied a fine article about a golden instrument.
explanation.walkthrough: Or is heraldry's word for gold, a convention worth learning; 'study' sounding like the spelling of a plant gives the first word.
explanation.definitionFit: A reed organ, such as a harmonium, sounds by air passing over vibrating metal reeds, a keyboard instrument.

clue.text: Aquatic mammal having excessive energy on river

blocks.note: OTT stands for over the top
E is the symbol for energy
R is the abbreviation for river

explanation.surface: A playful water creature has boundless energy along the riverbank.
explanation.walkthrough: 'On' in a down clue just means the pieces stack in order: OTT, E, then R.
explanation.definitionFit: Otters are semi-aquatic carnivores of rivers and coasts, and certainly mammals.

clue.text: Type of paint Gloria half used outside in stages

indicators.note: half of a word is kept, so the rest of it is cut away
the outside of a word is its edge, so only its two end letters are kept

blocks.note: half the six-letter name: its first three letters kept, the rest deleted
first and last letters of the word

explanation.surface: A decorator called Gloria applied a sort of paint outdoors in phases.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Used outside' reads as exterior paint, but 'used' only links and 'outside in stages' takes the end letters.
explanation.definitionFit: Gloss is a shiny, hard-wearing finish of paint, contrasting with matt or emulsion.

clue.text: Game I lost unfortunately leading to a rage

indicators.note: an unfortunate outcome is things going wrong, so the letters fall out of order

blocks.note: taken as written
taken as written
ire is anger

explanation.surface: A sore loser flies into a temper after losing a game.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Rage' is not anagram fodder; it supplies its synonym IRE.
explanation.definitionFit: Solitaire is a card or peg game played alone, also called patience.

clue.text: Vulgar animal noise

blocks.note: first meaning: crude, coarse, base
second meaning: the moo of a cow

explanation.walkthrough: Read together it sounds like a rude grunt; the two parts are separate meanings.
explanation.definitionFit: The word is an adjective for coarse or base behaviour and a noun for the deep sound cattle make.

clue.text: Son Kelvin that is heading for ruin — someone going downhill fast?

indicators.note: a heading is what stands at the top, so just the opening letter is used

blocks.note: S is the abbreviation for son
K is the symbol for kelvin, the temperature unit
i.e. abbreviates id est, Latin for that is
the opening letter of the word

explanation.surface: A son named Kelvin is on the road to ruin, sliding rapidly downhill in life.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Going downhill fast' looks like decline, but the question mark signals the literal sense: speeding down a slope.
explanation.definitionFit: A skier travels down snowy slopes at speed, literally descending quickly, so the playful description fits.

clue.text: Total in writing correct

blocks.note: something put in writing is put down on paper
right means correct

explanation.surface: An accountant checks that a written sum is right.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Total' tempts as a sum, but it is the adjective meaning utter.
explanation.definitionFit: Downright and total are both intensifying adjectives meaning complete or utter, as in a downright lie.
